title: Revisiting mental accounting classic paradigms: Replication Registered Report of the problems reviewed in Thaler (1999)

source.title: Revisiting mental accounting classic paradigms: Replication Registered Report of the problems reviewed in Thaler (1999)

studies.title: Unified online replication survey: Problems 1–21
studies.description: One data collection (N = 1007) in which each participant answered 9 of 18 Qualtrics blocks covering the 17 replicated problems and 4 extension problems. The problems draw on different original studies but share one replication survey and one protocol scope.

nodes.title: Replication Registered Report of the 17 mental-accounting problems in Thaler (1999), plus four extensions

fields.label: Method type
fields.value: Registered Report; online between-, within-, mixed-design and one-sample vignette/choice problems answered by US MTurk participants (CloudResearch); 18 Qualtrics blocks, each participant randomised into 9

fields.label: Summary
fields.value: The authors replicate 17 classic problems reviewed in Thaler (1999) and test four further predictions from the review, using one unified online survey (N = 1007, about 500 per problem). They report 11 problems with empirical support, three with mixed support and three without support, and for the four extensions support for two, mixed support for one and none for one.

nodes.title: Mental accounting and the choice of Thaler (1999)

fields.label: Question
fields.value: Do the classic mental-accounting demonstrations reviewed in Thaler (1999) replicate in a well-powered, pre-registered, independent online replication, and do four untested predictions of the review hold?

fields.label: Theory
fields.value: Mental accounting is the internal categorization system individuals adopt to manage their financial activities; it may result in suboptimal decisions or decisions not aligned with one’s own goals.

fields.label: Gap
fields.value: Several of the original problems did not report basic methodological details like sample size or descriptives, and statistical analyses were often not conducted or not reported in sufficient detail for reproducibility.

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: H1: people are risk-averse for gains and risk-seeking for losses.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 1 (Risk taking); replication of a problem reviewed in Thaler (1999)

nodes.title: H2: Time investment versus price reference point

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: H2: people are more likely to spend 20 minutes to save $5 out of $15 than to save $5 out of $125.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 2 (Time investment versus price reference point); replication of a problem reviewed in Thaler (1999)

fields.label: Hypothesis reconstructed by Li and Feldman
fields.value: People are more willing to buy a ticket when they have lost an equivalent amount of cash than when they lost their ticket (different mental accounts).

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 3 (Theatre play ticket); replication of a problem reviewed in Thaler (1999)

fields.label: Explicit hypothesis from the original problem
Statement
fields.value: H4: people follow four principles (a) segregate gains, (b) integrate loss, (c) cancel smaller losses against larger gains and (d) segregate ‘silver linings’ (small gains) from larger losses.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 4 (Events and happiness (hedonic framing)); replication of a problem reviewed in Thaler (1999)

nodes.title: H5: Same day or two weeks apart

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: H5: people choose to have the events occur ‘apart’ when segregation is preferred, and ‘together’ when integration is hedonically optimal.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 5 (Same day or two weeks apart); replication of a problem reviewed in Thaler (1999)

fields.label: Hypothesis reconstructed by Li and Feldman
fields.value: People integrate subsequent losses with prior gains but not with prior losses. Also, people are not very sensitive to the exact value of the prior losses when they are within the same magnitude as subsequent losses.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 6 (Emotional impact of losing $9); replication of a problem reviewed in Thaler (1999)

fields.label: Explicit hypothesis from the original problem
Statement
fields.value: H7: people are willing to pay more for the same product if bought from a resort than if bought from a grocery store.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 7 (Location and price); replication of a problem reviewed in Thaler (1999)

fields.label: Hypothesis reconstructed by Li and Feldman
fields.value: People request a price equal to cost when selling to a friend and a price equal to market price when selling to a stranger, unless their cost exceeds market price.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 8 (Selling ticket); replication of a problem reviewed in Thaler (1999)

fields.label: Explicit hypothesis from the original problem
Hypothesis reconstructed by Li and Feldman
fields.value: People exhibit a lack of consensus regarding the perception of the cost.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 9 (Wine bottle); replication of a problem reviewed in Thaler (1999)

fields.label: Explicit hypothesis from the original problem
Hypothesis reconstructed by Li and Feldman
fields.value: People are more agreeable with the view that the wine purchase is an investment.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 10 (Feelings about purchase); replication of a problem reviewed in Thaler (1999)

fields.label: Explicit hypothesis from the original problem

nodes.title: H11: Previous events and new payment

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: H11a: the budget-setting process promotes greater underconsumption in the $50 condition than the $20 condition. H11b: the expense-tracking process promotes greater underconsumption for related purchases.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 11 (Previous events and new payment); replication of a problem reviewed in Thaler (1999)

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: H12: subjects are willing to pay more money to avoid waiting the same amount of time for a higher-priced food or service than for a lower-priced product.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 12 (The performance (waiting time)); replication of a problem reviewed in Thaler (1999)

nodes.title: H13: Prior gain and risky choice

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: H13: the ‘house money’ effect—prior gain stimulates risk seeking.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 13 (Prior gain and risky choice); replication of a problem reviewed in Thaler (1999)

nodes.title: H14: Prior loss with loss potential

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: H14−H15: weaker to no effects for prior loss unless the gamble offers a chance to break even.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 14 (Prior loss with loss potential); replication of a problem reviewed in Thaler (1999)

nodes.title: H15: Prior loss without loss potential

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: H14−H15: weaker to no effects for prior loss unless the gamble offers a chance to break even.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 15 (Prior loss without loss potential); replication of a problem reviewed in Thaler (1999)

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: H16: people shift between single gambles and long-term repeating gambles.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 16 (Coin flip bet); replication of a problem reviewed in Thaler (1999)

fields.label: Hypothesis reconstructed by Li and Feldman
fields.value: People are less willing to undertake a single risky investment, but more willing to undertake a portfolio of 25 investments.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 17 (Division investment); replication of a problem reviewed in Thaler (1999)

fields.label: Explicit hypothesis from the original problem
Statement
fields.value: H18: if the family pays for the tickets, they will tend to go despite the weather. If the tickets are given to them, they will tend to stay home.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 18 (Game in bad weather); extension of a prediction made in Thaler (1999) or its sources

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: H19: purchasing membership will lead to continued play despite pain.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 19 (Membership and tennis elbow); extension of a prediction made in Thaler (1999) or its sources

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: H20: the more one paid for the shoes, the more times one will try to wear them. Eventually, one stops trying. But the more one paid, the longer one will keep the shoes before throwing them away.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 20 (Price and decision (shoes)); extension of a prediction made in Thaler (1999) or its sources

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: H21: membership phrased as ‘merely 27 cents a day’ will be more attractive.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Problem 21 (Annual membership (pennies-a-day)); extension of a prediction made in Thaler (1999) or its sources

fields.label: Human result
fields.value: 84% chose the sure gain (209/250) and 44% chose the sure loss (112/254). The remaining 56% in the loss condition chose the gamble. The gain/loss contrast supported the predicted framing effect (χ²(1) = 85.03, p < .001, Cramér’s V = .41).

fields.label: Human result
fields.value: The authors found no clear evidence of the expected reference-price effect. Only 11% in the $15 condition and 7% in the $125 condition would travel to save $5 (p = .066, Cramér’s V = .07).

fields.label: Human result
fields.value: 90% would buy a ticket after losing $10 in cash, compared with 77% after losing a ticket (p < .001, Cramér’s V = .17). The result supports the prediction that replacing a loss in the same mental account is less attractive.

fields.label: Human result
fields.value: All four choices favored the predicted way of grouping gains and losses. Cramér’s V ranged from .23 to .43. The authors note that more participants were indifferent than in the original study.

fields.label: Human result
fields.value: Participants rated same-day losses as less upsetting than losses two weeks apart in both loss scenarios. The gain scenario went in the opposite direction from the original prediction (Cramér’s V = .09).

fields.label: Human result
fields.value: Seven comparisons went in the predicted direction and three went in the opposite direction. A later $9 loss hurt less after a prior gain. It usually hurt more after a prior loss, including after a $1,000 loss compared with a $30 loss, opposite the original ordering.

fields.label: Human result
fields.value: Participants would pay more for the same soda at a fancy resort than at a grocery store (t(506) = 2.30, p = .011, d = .20).

fields.label: Human result
fields.value: Asking prices tracked the purchase price more closely for friends and the going market price more closely for strangers. Both prices influenced both types of sale. The authors reported a buyer effect (F = 594.75) and a three-way buyer × cost × market-price interaction (F = 19.51 in the prose, both p < .001).

fields.label: Human result
fields.value: Wine-cost perceptions differed from a benchmark in which an imagined comparison group all chose the current $75 market price. The authors found no clear difference in how people perceived the cost when giving the bottle away versus drinking it (χ²(4) = 3.64, p = .457).

fields.label: Human result
fields.value: Participants agreed more with describing the wine purchase as a $400 investment (M = 3.56) than as spending $400 (M = 2.98) or saving $100 (M = 3.08). The reported repeated-measures ANOVA was F(2, 1002) = 25.26.

fields.label: Human result
fields.value: Mental budgeting received mixed support. Buying an unrelated dinner left participants more willing to buy a theatre ticket than buying a sports ticket, at both spending levels ($50: d = .26; $20: d = .28). Paying for an unrelated flu vaccination produced no clear difference from the sports-ticket condition ($50: d = .04; $20: d = .05).

fields.label: Human result
fields.value: The amount offered above the ticket price to avoid waiting was higher in the $40 condition (M = $10.34) than the $15 condition (M = $8.14), d = .23, 95% CI [.04, .41].

fields.label: Human result
fields.value: Only 28% chose the gamble after a gain (P13), failing to support the house-money prediction. After a prior loss, 17% chose the gamble when it could add another loss (P14) and 24% when it could only add a gain (P15). The Stage 2 paired analyses found greater risk aversion in P14 than in P13 or P15 and no clear difference between P13 and P15. The paper classifies P14 as consistent with the original finding and P13 and P15 as inconsistent.

fields.label: Human result
fields.value: 25% accepted a single coin flip and 49% accepted a bundle of 100 flips. The result supports the prediction that bundling the bets makes them more attractive (Cohen’s g = .36).

fields.label: Human result
fields.value: 30% accepted a single project and 47% accepted the portfolio of 25 investments (Cohen’s g = .27), supporting the prediction that grouping projects increases risk taking.

fields.label: Human result
fields.value: 32% would attend the game during the storm when they paid $40 for the ticket versus 14% when it was a gift. The paid-ticket condition supported the prediction (Cohen’s g = .47 as reported).

fields.label: Human result
fields.value: 76% chose to stop playing tennis after developing pain despite paying for membership. The result was opposite the prediction that paying would lead them to continue (χ² = 132.60, p < .001).

fields.label: Human result
fields.value: Participants endorsed keeping the uncomfortable shoes longer (d = .33, p < .001). Evidence for wearing them more often was inconclusive (d = .07, 95% CI [−.01, .16]). Keeping received stronger endorsement than wearing in a paired comparison (dz = .19, p < .001). The article contains conflicting labels and p values for these results.

fields.label: Human result
fields.value: The daily fee looked more attractive than the annual fee. The contrast appeared both when participants saw one framing (mean 44.53 vs. 26.04, d = .61) and when they rated both (mean 45.16 vs. 35.72, dz = .29).

nodes.title: Overall finding: most classic mental-accounting effects replicate, some are more contextual

fields.label: Answer
fields.value: We successfully replicated 11 problems, found mixed support for three problems and failed to find support for three problems, suggesting that mental accounting effects generally tend to replicate well but that some effects may be more complex and contextual than originally documented.

fields.label: Support
fields.value: We concluded a mostly successful replication: out of the 17 problems, we found empirical support for 11, mixed empirical support for three and no empirical support for three. Extending the replication, we provided an initial test of four untested predictions described in Thaler 1999 J. Behav. Decis. Mak. 12, 183–206. (doi: 10.1002/(SICI)1099-0771(199909)12:33.0.CO;2-F), of which we found empirical support for two, mixed support for one and no support for one.

fields.label: Validity
fields.value: Original studies often reported only descriptive statistics, so the authors deduced a set of statistical analyses; they caution against over-interpreting comparisons with the original effects.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Participants were exclusively from the United States and recruited on an online platform; data were collected during the COVID-19 pandemic.

fields.label: Limitations
fields.value: Generalizability limited by the US online sample and pandemic timing; adjustments to the original problems (soda for beer, discounted tickets, added statements) and the unified design.

fields.label: Replications
fields.value: The paper mentions a multi-country mass collaboration (Priolo et al.) that released findings with results very similar to those reported.

fields.label: Openness
fields.value: All materials, data and code are on the Open Science Framework.

nodes.title: Main analysis sample and replication evaluation

fields.label: Analysis and sample
fields.value: The authors used R 4.3.2 and the JAMOVI jmv package. Their preregistered main analysis used all survey completers. Problem-specific denominators follow the block assignment.

fields.label: Evaluating replication
fields.value: The authors applied LeBel et al.’s criteria to compare signal, direction and effect sizes. In cases where an original effect size could not be recovered, they used signal/no signal and direction.

In a Registered Report with an online US sample recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk using CloudResearch, we conducted a replication of 17 classic problems reviewed in Thaler 1999

We concluded a mostly successful replication: out of the 17 problems, we found empirical support for 11, mixed empirical support for three and no empirical support for three. Extending the replication, we provided an initial test of four untested predictions described in Thaler 1999 J. Behav. Decis. Mak. 12, 183–206. (doi: 10.1002/(SICI)1099-0771(199909)12:33.0.CO;2-F), of which we found empirical support for two, mixed support for one and no support for one.

We used the following CloudResearch options: Duplicate IP Block, Duplicate Geocode Block, Suspicious Geocode Block, Verify Worker Country Location, Enhanced Privacy, CloudResearch Approved Participants, Block Low Quality Participants, etc.
The display of problems and conditions was counterbalanced using the randomizer ‘evenly present’ function in Qualtrics.

We summarized the experimental designs in table 4 . We mapped the designs used in the problems, which included one-sample, between-subject, within-subject and mixed experimental designs. We set up all the problems using Qualtrics. We had a total of 18 Qualtrics blocks, and empirically related problems were grouped in a single Qualtrics block so that the same participants answered all related problems: (i) Problems 13, 14 and 15, and (ii) Problems 18 and 19.

Problems 1–3, 6–9, 11, 12 and 21 involved between-subjects manipulations, and participants were randomly assigned to conditions separately in each of those. The order of the problems was also randomized.

among the problems we aimed to replicate, several did not report basic methodological details like sample size or descriptives. Statistical analyses were also often not conducted or not reported in sufficient detail for reproducibility.

We aimed to compare the replication effects with the effects in the original studies using the criteria set by LeBel et al. [36].

In our replication of Problem 1, we found support for Tversky and Kahneman’s [ 13] findings that people were more risk-averse for gains (84%) than for losses (56%; χ²(1) = 85.03, p < 0.001; Cramer’s V = 0.41 [0.32, 0.50]).

In our replication of Problem 2, we failed to find support for Tversky and Kahneman’s [6] findings that people were more inclined to spend 20 min to save $5 out of $15 (save $5 out of $15: 11%; save $5 out of $125: 7%; χ²(1) = 3.39, p = 0.066; Cramer’s V = 0.07 [0.00, 0.17]).

In our replication of Problem 3, we found support for Tversky and Kahneman‘s [ 6] findings that sunk costs impact decisions less when sunk costs are not from the same mental account (90% bought ticket after losing $10), compared with when sunk costs are from the same mental account (77% bought ticket after losing a ticket; χ²(1) = 16.18, p < 0.001; Cramer’s V = 0.17 [0.09, 0.27]).

In our replication of Problem 4, we found support for Thaler’s [ 9] findings that people prefer to segregate gains (Cramer’s V = 0.26 [0.20, 0.33]), integrate losses (Cramer’s V = 0.23 [0.17, 0.29]), integrate smaller losses with larger gains (Cramer’s V = 0.43 [0.37, 0.49]), and segregate small gains from large losses (Cramer’s V = 0.31 [0.25, 0.37]). Effects were consistent with yet weaker than the original studies, and a larger proportion of the participants in the replication were indifferent.

In our replication of Problem 5, we found support for Thaler and Johnson’s [ 8] findings that integrated losses were less upsetting than separate losses (5B: Cramer’s V = 0.28 [0.21, 0.34]; 5C: Cramer’s V = 0.23 [0.17, 0.29]), but opposite findings to the original’s that separate gains were happier than integrated gains (5A: Cramer’s V = 0.09 [0.03, 0.16]).

In our replication of Problem 6, we found some support for Thaler and Johnson’s [ 8] findings: seven effects replicated well with larger effects, whereas three effects were in the opposite direction. Participants perceived the loss of $9 as less upsetting when it occurs after a prior gain (Cramer’s V = 0.50 [0.41, 0.59]), but as more upsetting if the $9 loss followed prior losses, yet—inconsistent with the target article —the magnitude of the prior losses did not seem to have much impact (Cramer’s V = 0.47–0.60). When prior losses were compared directly in the comparison between losing $9 after a loss of either $30 or $1000, participants perceived the loss following $1000 to be more painful, opposite from the target’s findings. Regardless of the comparison between which hurts more, the core argument is that people are not indifferent to prior losses , and our findings support this idea—participants indicated that they think they would not ignore prior losses and integrate this in their evaluations of loss.

In our replication of Problem 7, we found support for Thaler’s [ 9] findings that people are willing to adjust their spending based on the purchasing context. People were willing to pay higher prices for the same soda in a fancy resort hotel than in a grocery store ( t(506) = 2.30, p = 0.011; Cohen’s d = 0.20 [0.03, 0.38]).

In our replication of Problem 8, we found support for Thaler’s [ 9] findings that people request a price equal to cost when selling to a friend and a price equal to market price when selling to a stranger (unless their cost exceeds market price) (friend versus stranger: F = 594.75, p <0.001, η²p = 0.55 [0.49, 0.59]; interaction of the three factors—buyer, cost, and market price: F = 19.51, p < 0.001, η²p = 0.07 [0.03, 0.12]).

In our replication of Problem 9, we found support for Shafir and Thaler’s, 1998, unpublished data, findings that people’s estimation of the cost of a bottle of wine—which gains value over time—differs from a rational economic assessment in which the cost reflects current market price (giving away: χ²(4) = 333, p < 0.001, Cramer’s V = 0.81 [0.72, 0.89]; drinking: χ²(4) = 298, p < 0.001, Cramer’s V = 0.77 [0.68, 0.85]; comparing giving away versus drinking: χ²(4) = 3.64, p = 0.457, Cramer’s V = 0.00 [0.00, 0.14]).

In our replication of Problem 10, we found support for Shafir and Thaler’s, 1998, unpublished data, findings that people tend to perceive the wine purchase as an investment (spent $400: M = 2.98, s.d.= 1.45; invest $400: M = 3.56, s.d. = 1.30; save $100: M = 3.08, s.d. = 1.36; F(2, 1002) = 25.26, η²p = 0.05).

We carried out a well-powered Registered Report to replicate and extend classic decision-making and behavioural economics problems that were reviewed by Thaler [ 1] on or related to the topic of mental accounting. More than 26 years after the publication of Thaler’s review paper, in our replication, we were able to find support for 11 out of the 17 problems reviewed. Specifically, we found consistent results for Problems 1, 3, 4, 7–9, 10, 12, 14, 16 and 17. Yet, the results for Problems 5, 6 and 11 were mixed, and the results of Problems 2, 13 and 15 were inconsistent with the original findings.
